This interpretation is objected to because jihad was obligated in Medina. Abu al-Samal recited "faraghat" with a kasra on the ra', and it is a dialect. Some recited "fa-inshabba" with a shadda on the ba' and a fatha, and its meaning is: when you finish from jihad, "fa-inshabba" toward Medina. Al-Naqqash mentioned it, noting that it is an error. Others, the Imamiyya, recited "fa-insib" with a kasra on the sad, meaning: when you finish the matter of prophethood, then appoint a successor (khalifa). This is an anomalous reading, weak in meaning, not established on any scholar. Shurayh passed by two men wrestling and said: this is not the matter of finishing, and recited this verse.

His saying, exalted: ﴿and to your Lord direct your longing﴾ is a command to rely upon God, Mighty and Majestic, and to turn the directions of one's desires toward Him alone and not to anything else. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "fa-raghghib" with a fatha on the ra' and a shadda on the ghayn with a kasra.

The exegesis of Surat al-Sharh is complete, and praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.

(p-643) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Sharh

It is Meccan, by the consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun), with no disagreement among them on this.

God, Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ ﴿And We removed from you your burden,﴾ ﴿which had weighed down your back,﴾ ﴿and We exalted your remembrance for you.﴾ ﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease;﴾ ﴿indeed, with hardship comes ease.﴾ ﴿So when you are free, then labor,﴾ ﴿and to your Lord direct your longing.﴾

God enumerated to His Prophet (ﷺ) His blessings in that He expanded his breast for prophethood and prepared him for it. The majority of scholars hold that this expansion of the breast means illuminating it with wisdom and widening it to receive what is revealed to him. Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him) and a group said: this is a reference to his being opened up by Jibril (peace be upon him) when he was a child and during the Night Journey (isra'), since tashrih (dissection) means cutting the flesh. Abu Ja'far al-Mansur recited "Did We not expand (alam nashrah)" with a fatha on the ha', in the manner of the poet's saying:

"Drive away from yourself the worries that approach you, as you strike with the sword the forehead of the horse."

Similar to it in Abu Zayd's Nawadir is:

"From which of my two days do I flee from death? A day not decreed, or a day that is decreed?"

It is as if He, exalted, said: "Did We not expand (nashrahann)," then the nun was changed to an alif, then it was dropped for lightness. This reading is rejected.

(p-644) The "burden" (wizr) that God removed from him, according to some of those who interpreted it, is the weight and distress that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) experienced before the mission (ba'tha), when he saw the evil that Quraysh was engaged in through the worship of idols, and no clear command had come to him from God. So God removed that weight from him by His prophethood and sending. Abu 'Ubayda and others said the meaning is: We lightened for you the burdens of prophethood and helped you against the people. Qatada, Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, and most of the exegetes said: the wizr here is sins; the weight is used as a figure for sins. This verse is similar to His saying: ﴿that God may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what followed﴾ [al-Fath: 2]. In the Jahiliyya before prophethood, the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) burden was keeping company with his people, eating from their sacrificial animals, and the like. Al-Dahhak, and in the book of al-Naqqash, said: it was his presence with his people at gatherings that God does not love.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

All of these are drawn from the (natural) upbringing (al-mansha'), like his witnessing the War of the Fujjar, when he would hurl stones at his uncles, while his heart in that was turned in repentance toward what is right. As for the worship of idols, he never became entangled with it at all. Anas ibn Malik recited: "And We lowered from you your burden (wahattatna 'anka wizrak)," and in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "And We unloaded from you your load (wahallalna 'anka wiqrak)," and in the codex of Ubayy: "And We lowered from you your load (wahattatna 'anka wiqrak)." Abu 'Amr mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) approved all of them. Al-Muhasibi said: the sins of the prophets (peace be upon them) are described as a weight, and they are minor sins that are forgiven, because of their concern about them and their regret over them.

(p-645) "Anqada" means: made it a fracture (naqd), i.e., weak and defective from the weight. It is also said its meaning is: made him hear a creaking (naqid), which is the sound, like the creaking of ships. Whatever you load with a weight, it creaks beneath it. 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"And what I bore of them broke my back, though I was compassionate toward them, tender-hearted."

His saying, exalted: ﴿and We exalted your remembrance for you﴾ means: We made your name famous, and carried it to every place on earth, while the Messenger of God was in Mecca. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatada said: the meaning of His saying ﴿and We exalted your remembrance for you﴾ is: We joined your name with Our name in the call to prayer (adhan) and the sermons. A tradition is related on this: "God, exalted, said: when I am mentioned, you are mentioned with Me." This suggests the verse was revealed in Mecca early, while the adhan was legislated in Medina. Raising the remembrance is a blessing upon the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace). Likewise, it is a beauty and a good for those who manage the affairs of people, while obscurity of name and renown is good for those who are solitary in worship. God, exalted, has made blessings into divisions according to what suits each individual. In a hadith: "God, exalted, will make a servant stand on the Day of Resurrection and say: Did I not do for you such and such? He enumerates for him his blessings, and says among them: Did I not make your name most obscure among the people?" The meaning of this enumeration addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) is: O Muhammad, We have given you all of this, so do not be troubled by the harm of Quraysh, for the One who bestowed these blessings upon you will grant you victory over them and help you against them.

Then He strengthened his hope with His saying, glorified be He: ﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾, meaning: what you see of harm is a relief that will come to you. God repeated this for emphasis and clarification of the good. Some people said the meaning is: indeed with hardship comes ease in this world, and indeed with hardship comes ease in the Hereafter. Many scholars held that with every hardship there are two eases from this verse, since "hardship" (al-'usr) is definite by reference to a previous mention, while "ease" (al-yusr) is indefinite, so the first is other than the second. A hadith has been related on this interpretation from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "One hardship will never overcome two eases." As for the statement of 'Umar concerning it, it is explicit in the Muwatta' in his letter to Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah (may God be pleased with them both). 'Isa, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and Abu Ja'far recited "al-'usru, al-yusru" with two dammas. Ibn Mas'ud recited "Indeed with hardship is ease (yusran)" once, not repeated.

Then His Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was commanded that when he finished some task of the affairs of prophethood and worship, he should strive (yansab) in another, and nasab means fatigue. The meaning is that he should persist in what he was commanded and not slacken. Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him) said: the meaning is: when you finish your obligatory duty, then strive in voluntary worship as worship to your Lord. Ibn Mas'ud said: strive in the night prayer (qiyam al-layl). From Mujahid: when you finish with the business of your worldly life, then strive in the worship of your Lord. It is also said the meaning is: when you finish the units of prayer, sit in the tashahhud and strive in supplication. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: the meaning of the speech is: when you finish worship, then strive in supplication. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: when you finish jihad, then strive in worship. This interpretation is objected to because jihad was obligated in Medina. Abu al-Samal recited "faraghat" with a kasra on the ra', and it is a dialect. Some recited "fa-inshabba" with a shadda on the ba' and a fatha, and its meaning is: when you finish from jihad, "fa-inshabba" toward Medina. Al-Naqqash mentioned it, noting that it is an error. Others, the Imamiyya, recited "fa-insib" with a kasra on the sad, meaning: when you finish the matter of prophethood, then appoint a successor (khalifa). This is an anomalous reading, weak in meaning, not established on any scholar. Shurayh passed by two men wrestling and said: this is not the matter of finishing, and recited this verse.

His saying, exalted: ﴿and to your Lord direct your longing﴾ is a command to rely upon God, Mighty and Majestic, and to turn the directions of one's desires toward Him alone and not to anything else. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "fa-raghghib" with a fatha on the ra' and a shadda on the ghayn with a kasra.

The exegesis of Surat al-Sharh is complete, and praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.
